# Topic at a Glance

> **One-sentence summary:** A de Bruijn graph represents observed k-mer overlaps as graph edges, so assembling a genome becomes finding sequence-consistent paths through that graph.

| Item | Description |
|---|---|
| **Biological question** | What genomic sequence is supported by a collection of sequencing reads? |
| **Computational problem** | Reconstruct long strings from many short, noisy, overlapping substrings |
| **Method type** | Graph-based assembly |
| **Typical input** | Quality-controlled short or long reads, usually after error correction |
| **Typical output** | Contigs, unitigs, assembly graph, and sometimes scaffolds |
| **Prerequisites** | [k-mers and sequence composition](k-mers-and-sequence-composition.qmd), reverse complements, graph paths |

# From reads to a graph

A read set contains many overlapping observations of the same genome. Comparing every read pair is costly, particularly for short-read data. A de Bruijn graph instead shares the overlaps implicitly through k-mers.

For each observed k-mer, create a directed edge from its prefix of length $k-1$ to its suffix of length $k-1$. Consecutive k-mers overlap by $k-1$ bases, so a walk spells a sequence by appending one base per traversed edge.

```text
k-mer: ACGT
node:  ACG  ->  CGT

ACG -> CGT -> GTA
      spells ACGTA
```

This is a compact form of the overlap information already present in the read set. It is related to the fixed-word representation in [k-mers and sequence composition](k-mers-and-sequence-composition.qmd), but here each word is placed in a connectivity structure rather than treated as an independent count.

# Assembly as graph traversal

## Build, clean, compact

1. **Extract k-mers.** Split reads at ambiguous bases and apply a defined reverse-complement convention. Usually retain abundance information.
2. **Build edges.** Add prefix-to-suffix edges for trusted k-mers. Edge multiplicity can approximate coverage.
3. **Remove likely artifacts.** Sequencing errors create low-abundance tips, bubbles, and disconnected components. Simplification uses coverage, read evidence, and graph topology; it must not automatically erase real low-coverage or heterozygous sequence.
4. **Compact non-branching paths.** A maximal path whose internal nodes have one incoming and one outgoing edge becomes a **unitig**, reducing the graph while preserving its sequence.
5. **Traverse resolvable paths.** Branches caused by repeats or variants may remain as alternative paths. Assemblers emit unambiguous contigs and may use paired reads or long reads to resolve remaining connections.

In an ideal error-free graph, reconstructing all edge labels is an Eulerian-path problem: a valid traversal uses each observed k-mer edge in an appropriate multiplicity. Real assembly adds errors, variable coverage, repeats, and diploidy, so production assemblers solve a constrained graph-cleaning and path-selection problem rather than a single textbook Euler tour.

# A toy example

Let $k=3$ and suppose the trusted k-mers are `ATG`, `TGA`, and `GAT`.

```text
AT -> TG -> GA -> AT
 edge  edge  edge

one circular spelling: ATGAT
```

Each edge supplies the next base after a two-base overlap. If a second genomic region also contains `TGA`, its evidence merges at the same graph edge. Such merging is valuable compression, but it is also why repeats longer than the available unique context create unresolved branches.

# Choosing $k$ and interpreting branches

The choice of $k$ controls a familiar trade-off:

| Choice | Benefit | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Smaller $k$ | Connects through lower coverage and errors more readily | Collapses more repeats and increases spurious connectivity |
| Larger $k$ | Separates more repeats and reduces accidental overlaps | Breaks paths at errors or low coverage; needs more memory |

A branch is not automatically an error. It can represent a repeat, a heterozygous allele, strain variation, or contamination. Coverage, read-pair orientation, long-read spans, and biological expectations help distinguish these cases. In diploid or metagenomic samples, forcing every bubble into one path can destroy meaningful variation.

# Practical workflow

Short-read assemblers such as [SPAdes](https://ablab.github.io/spades/) and [MEGAHIT](https://github.com/voutcn/megahit) use de Bruijn-graph ideas, typically with multi-$k$ strategies and extensive graph processing. A minimal conceptual workflow is:

```text
reads -> adapter/quality control -> error-aware k-mers -> de Bruijn graph
      -> simplify + compact -> contigs -> evaluate graph and assembly
```

Evaluate more than total assembly length. Inspect contiguity, read support, duplication, taxonomic contamination, and reference-based correctness where a suitable reference exists. Graph visualizers and assembly-graph formats can reveal repeat or heterozygosity structure that a contig-only FASTA hides.

# Limitations and connections

- **Repeats:** a repeat longer than the usable k-mer context creates ambiguity; long reads may bridge it.
- **Errors and uneven coverage:** both fragment or clutter the graph, especially with low-depth samples.
- **Memory:** storing many distinct k-mers is demanding for large or complex datasets; compact graph representations address this directly.
- **Loss of read linkage:** the basic graph forgets which distant k-mers came from the same read. Read pairs, long reads, and linked reads restore some of that information.

de Bruijn graphs are usually preferable to all-pairs overlap construction for large short-read collections. For long, accurate reads, [overlap--layout--consensus assembly](overlap-layout-consensus-assembly.qmd) can preserve long-range read structure more naturally. Minimizer sketches from [minimizers and sequence sketching](minimizers-and-sequence-sketching.qmd) are often used to make overlap discovery or graph indexing scalable.

# Take-home Messages

1. A de Bruijn graph turns k-mer overlaps into directed edges and spells sequences as paths.
2. Unitigs preserve unambiguous sequence while exposing unresolved repeat and variant structure.
3. $k$, error handling, and graph simplification are biological as well as computational choices.
4. A contig is a path supported by the graph, not proof that every repeat or haplotype was resolved.
